```{r setup}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ggcircos)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(20260101)
```

## What a track is

A **track** is a radial band drawn just outside the node ring, holding one
small plot per node. Every node of the ring gets its own slot in the band,
and the value you have for that node decides how far the slot reaches: a
column, a bar, an area, a boxplot, a point, a tile or a piece of text.

`circlize` does this with a second drawing model. Its canvas is painted
directly, so a track is a separate drawing call that needs its own clipping
region, its own scale and its own axis, and the values have to be
normalised by hand against the band's radii before they are handed over.

`ggcircos` keeps the same idea but stores it as data. The band is declared
up front, its radius interval becomes part of the layout, and normalising a
value into that interval is the job of a *position* -- the same kind of
object ggplot2 uses for `geom_bar()`. A track is therefore an ordinary
ggplot2 layer: it can be faceted, it can carry a legend, and it obeys the
same scales and themes as everything else on the plot.

Two things follow from that and are worth remembering while reading the
rest of this vignette:

* the layout is computed once and never touched again, so a track cannot
  disagree with the ring it is attached to;
* `ggcircos()` adds no layer of its own -- a plot without a geom draws
  nothing.

## One track

A track needs three things: a band declared in the layout, a data frame
with one value per node, and the name of the column that holds the node
ids.

```{r one-track-data}
m <- cor(mtcars)

gc <- data.frame(
  id = colnames(mtcars),
  gc = runif(ncol(mtcars))
)
head(gc)
```

The band is declared with `tracks`, a named vector of widths measured in
radii of the node ring. `track_offset` is the gap between the ring and the
first band; the default of 0.02 would put the band right on top of the
node arcs, so it is widened here to leave room for the node labels.

```{r one-track-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "One track: a column per node, drawn in the band declared by `tracks = c(gc = 0.12)`."}
p_one <- ggcircos(
  m,
  order = "hclust",
  tracks = c(gc = 0.12),
  track_offset = 0.12
) +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) +
  geom_track(
    data = gc,
    aes(x = gc),
    node = id,
    geom = "col",
    band = "gc",
    fill = "grey70",
    colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0
  )
p_one
```

Four parts of that call carry the whole idea:

* **`tracks = c(gc = 0.12)`** declares the band and gives it a name. The
  name is what a layer refers to later. A band that was never declared is
  an error: `Unknown track "gc". Declared tracks: ...`.
* **`band = "gc"`** says which declared band this layer draws into. It can
  also be an explicit radius interval, `c(r0, r1)`, for a band that no
  layer shares.
* **`node = id`** is the *unquoted name of a column*, not a value. The
  layer reads the ids out of that column and turns them into angles, using
  the layout. Writing `node = "id"` (a string) or `node = gc` (the column
  of values) does not do what it looks like.
* **`aes(x = gc)`** maps the value that gets scaled into the band. The
  scale is applied by the position, not by a ggplot2 axis, which is why
  the band's own axis has to be asked for separately (see below).

`geom = "col"` draws an anchored column: the bar starts at the inner edge
of the band and ends at the scaled value. `"area"` and `"bar"` behave the
same way; `"point"`, `"text"` and `"tile"` sit at a radius instead of
growing out of the inner edge.

The band is a plain data frame like everything else, and the layout of the
plot can be asked for it:

```{r one-track-layout}
lay <- circos_layout_of(p_one)
layout_tracks(lay)
```

`r0` and `r1` are the inner and outer radius of the band. They are the
numbers the position maps values into, and they are why the same `gc`
value lands at the same radius in every plot that uses the same layout.

## Two tracks and an axis

A second band is declared the same way, and each band gets its own layer.
`scales = "fixed"` with explicit `limits` puts both bands on one scale,
so the two tracks can be compared and the axis can mean something.

```{r two-tracks-plot, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 7, fig.cap = "Two tracks and a radial axis. The axis stands in the gap before the first node and labels the `gc` band; the `depth` band uses the same 0-1 scale."}
depth <- data.frame(
  id = colnames(mtcars),
  depth = runif(ncol(mtcars), 0.05, 0.40)
)

p_two <- ggcircos(
  m,
  order = "hclust",
  tracks = c(gc = 0.12, depth = 0.12),
  track_offset = 0.12
) +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) +
  geom_track(
    data = gc, aes(x = gc), node = id, geom = "col", band = "gc",
    scales = "fixed", limits = c(0, 1),
    fill = "grey70", colour = "grey30"
  ) +
  geom_track(
    data = depth, aes(x = depth), node = id, geom = "col", band = "depth",
    scales = "fixed", limits = c(0, 1),
    fill = "grey45", colour = "grey15"
  ) +
  geom_track_axis(band = "gc", limits = c(0, 1)) +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0
  )
p_two
```

The data behind the two layers is ordinary, and is worth looking at before
it is drawn:

```{r two-tracks-data}
head(gc)
head(depth)
```

The axis is a separate layer with its own geometry. It draws the two edges
of the band as rings, one short radial tick per break standing at the start
angle of the first node -- a gap, so the ticks never sit on a node arc --
and the break labels read tangentially, each at the radius of its own
break.

`limits` is required, and it is required for a reason: `geom_track_axis()`
is a layer of its own, and a layer cannot see the data of another layer.
Rather than guess the range of the `gc` track it would have to invent one,
so it refuses:

```{r axis-error}
msg <- tryCatch(
  ggcircos(m, tracks = c(gc = 0.12)) +
    geom_track(data = gc, aes(x = gc), node = id, geom = "col", band = "gc") +
    geom_track_axis(band = "gc"),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
cat(msg, "\n")
```

The error is raised when the layer is added, so it is caught while the
plot is being built rather than when it is drawn. The rule to remember is
short: give the axis the same `limits` you gave the track.

## Different scales per node

`geom_track()` needs to know where the band's inner edge and its outer
edge are, and therefore where a value sits between them. `scales` says
where the *value range* comes from.

`scales = "free"` (the default) infers it from the data: the baseline is
0 when every value is non-negative and the smallest value otherwise, and
the top of the range is the largest value in the layer. The track fills its
band, whatever the data happens to look like.

`scales = "fixed"` uses the `limits` you pass, and every value is mapped
through that pair. Use it when two tracks have to be read against each
other, or when an axis has to mean one thing across several layers.

```{r scales-plots, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "The same two tracks with a free scale (left) and a fixed 0-1 scale (right). Under the free scale each band is stretched to its own data, so `depth` looks as long as `gc`; under the fixed scale both bands use 0-1 and the difference is visible."}
track_pair <- function(scales, limits = NULL) {
  ggcircos(
    m,
    order = "hclust",
    tracks = c(gc = 0.12, depth = 0.12),
    track_offset = 0.12
  ) +
    geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) +
    geom_track(
      data = gc, aes(x = gc), node = id, geom = "col", band = "gc",
      scales = scales, limits = limits,
      fill = "grey70", colour = "grey30"
    ) +
    geom_track(
      data = depth, aes(x = depth), node = id, geom = "col", band = "depth",
      scales = scales, limits = limits,
      fill = "grey45", colour = "grey15"
    ) +
    geom_node_arc() +
    geom_node_text() +
    scale_fill_gradient2(
      low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0
    )
}

p_free <- track_pair("free")
p_fixed <- track_pair("fixed", c(0, 1))

grid::pushViewport(
  grid::viewport(layout = grid::grid.layout(nrow = 1, ncol = 2))
)
print(p_free, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 1))
print(p_fixed, vp = grid::viewport(layout.pos.row = 1, layout.pos.col = 2))
grid::popViewport()
```

The numbers behind the difference are the radii the position computed.
The built data keeps the order of the input rows:

```{r scales-numbers}
built_free <- ggplot_build(p_free)
built_fixed <- ggplot_build(p_fixed)

data.frame(
  id = depth$id,
  depth = round(depth$depth, 3),
  radius_free = round(built_free$data[[3]]$x, 4),
  radius_fixed = round(built_fixed$data[[3]]$x, 4)
)
```

One thing is worth spelling out, because it is easy to assume otherwise.
In 0.1.0 the range is taken from the layer's data *as a whole*, not from
each node separately: a node whose values cover a narrow range ends up with
a short bar even when another node in the same track reaches the edge of
the band. `scales = "fixed"` does not change that either -- it only
replaces the inferred range with one you declare. So `limits` is the tool
for comparing nodes against each other, and the per-node normalisation
that the documentation describes is not implemented yet.

Values outside `limits` are not clipped. They are mapped past the outer
edge of the band, and the plot's own radius limit squishes them at the
edge of the panel, so `limits` should cover the data.

## Facets

Faceting works because the layout is shared. A facet splits the *links*,
not the ring: the chord layer is cut into one set of links per panel, while
the node ring is the same ring in every panel.

The data for this section is four samples over six shared nodes. Each
sample has its own links, and `sample` is an ordinary column of the link
table, which is what the facet variable has to be.

```{r facet-data}
nodes <- c("A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F")
samples <- c("s1", "s2", "s3", "s4")

links <- do.call(rbind, lapply(samples, function(s) {
  pairs <- t(combn(sample(nodes, 4), 2))
  data.frame(
    from = pairs[, 1], to = pairs[, 2], sample = s,
    r = runif(nrow(pairs)),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}))
head(links)
```

```{r facet-plot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "One ring, four sets of links. The facet splits the chords; the node arcs and their labels are the same in every panel."}
p_facet <- ggcircos(links, order = "hclust") +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text() +
  facet_wrap(~ sample, nrow = 2) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b", midpoint = 0
  )
p_facet
```

`ggplot_build()` makes the structure visible. It returns **one data frame
per layer**, not one per panel; the `PANEL` column says which panel a row
belongs to.

```{r facet-build}
built <- ggplot_build(p_facet)

length(built$data)
vapply(built$data, nrow, integer(1))
```

The chord layer holds all 24 links at once, and the `PANEL` column splits
them into the four panels:

```{r facet-build-panels}
table(built$data[[1]]$PANEL)
```

The node ring holds no facet variable, so ggplot2 replicates it into every
panel -- six arcs per panel, at the same angles:

```{r facet-build-ring}
arc <- built$data[[2]]
table(arc$PANEL)
tapply(arc$y, arc$PANEL, function(theta) length(unique(theta)))
```

The same is true of a track layer whose data has no facet column: it is
replicated, so the ring and its tracks stay identical across panels while
the chords change. Give the track data a facet column of its own if the
tracks should differ per panel.

## Tiles

A tile track turns a node's arc into a sequence of bins. The rows of one
node are its bins, in the order they appear in the data, and they split the
arc evenly. The value is carried by colour, because a tile fills the band
radially instead of growing out of its inner edge.

```{r tiles-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "A tile track: four bins per node, coloured by their value. The chords are flat so that the fill scale belongs to the track."}
bins <- 4
heat <- data.frame(
  id = rep(colnames(mtcars), each = bins),
  value = runif(ncol(mtcars) * bins)
)
head(heat)

p_tiles <- ggcircos(
  m,
  order = "hclust",
  tracks = c(heat = 0.18),
  track_offset = 0.12
) +
  geom_chord(fill = "grey85") +
  geom_track(
    data = heat,
    aes(fill = value),
    node = id,
    geom = "tile",
    band = "heat"
  ) +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text() +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
    midpoint = 0.5, limits = c(0, 1)
  )
p_tiles
```

Two details are worth keeping in mind:

* the `x` aesthetic is a placeholder for a tile; the value belongs in
  `fill`, and the band is filled from `r0` to `r1` regardless;
* the fill scale belongs to whoever maps `fill`. Here the chords use a
  constant grey so that the gradient describes the track. ggplot2 has one
  fill scale per plot, so a plot that colours both the chords and the
  tiles by different quantities has to pick one of them to colour.

## Violins

A violin is the tile track's opposite case. A tile puts one value on the
band per bin; a violin puts a whole distribution there. With several
samples per node, `geom = "violin"` turns the usual violin on its side: the
value runs along the radius, and the density decides how much of the node's
arc the outline takes at that value. Each node gets its own outline,
centred on its arc and widest where its samples pile up.

```{r violin-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "A violin track: 40 samples per node, the density spread along each node's arc and the value along the radius."}
set.seed(1)
samples <- data.frame(
  id = rep(colnames(mtcars), each = 40),
  value = rnorm(ncol(mtcars) * 40, 0.5, 0.1)
)
head(samples)

p_violin <- ggcircos(
  m,
  order = "hclust",
  tracks = c(dist = 0.3),
  track_offset = 0.12
) +
  geom_chord(fill = "grey90") +
  geom_track(
    data = samples,
    aes(x = value),
    node = id,
    geom = "violin",
    band = "dist",
    fill = "steelblue",
    colour = NA,
    alpha = 0.85
  ) +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text()
p_violin
```

Three things behave differently from the other track geometries:

* the radius is still the position's job, so `scales`, `limits` and
  `baseline` apply exactly as they do to a column track: a violin is not a
  band-filling geometry;
* `n`, `adjust` and `trim` go to `stats::density()`: `n` is the number of
  density points, `adjust` multiplies the bandwidth, and `trim = FALSE`
  keeps the kernel's tails beyond the observed range;
* the density is spread over each node's **whole** arc, the way a boxplot's
  mark is, because the stat folds a node's rows into one mark. The bin
  split that a `col` or `tile` track uses does not apply.

A node needs at least three finite values with some spread to have a
density; a node that has none is skipped, and a layer where no node
qualifies warns instead of drawing an unexplained empty band.

## Density curves

`geom = "density"` draws the same density as the violin, but as an **open
curve** instead of a closed outline. Each curve leaves its node's centre line
and rises to that node's own mode, so the band reads as a ring of ridges.

Everything else -- `n`, `adjust`, `trim`, and the radial normalisation through
`scales`/`limits`/`baseline` -- behaves exactly as it does for the violin,
because both run the same kernel. The two differ only in closing the outline
or not, which is why this is a separate `geom` rather than a `fill = FALSE`
switch.

```{r density-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 6.5, fig.cap = "A density track: one open ridge per node, the density spread along the arc and the value along the radius. Nothing is filled, so the chords underneath stay readable."}
set.seed(3)
wide <- data.frame(
  id = rep(colnames(mtcars), each = 60),
  value = rnorm(ncol(mtcars) * 60, 0.55, 0.16)
)

p_density <- ggcircos(m, order = "hclust", tracks = c(dist = 0.35)) +
  geom_chord(fill = "grey92") +
  geom_track(
    data = wide,
    aes(x = value),
    node = id,
    geom = "density",
    band = "dist",
    colour = "steelblue",
    linewidth = 0.8
  ) +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text()
p_density
```

Two behaviours are worth knowing:

* the curve is **not closed**, so it has no `fill` worth setting; use
  `"violin"` when you want the shape filled;
* every curve is centred on its own node, so two subgroups of the *same* node
  drawn as two curves would be interleaved rather than stacked. Split them
  with `facet_wrap()` or give each its own band, the way you would with any
  other track geometry;
* a curve that runs past the angular seam is **split** there, not clipped.
  A polygon clip returns a ring whose edges lie on the seam, which is
  invisible for a fill but would draw a straight line along the seam for a
  stroke -- so the curve is cut into pieces and continued on the other side.

Both geometries need at least three finite values with some spread per node;
a node that has none is skipped, and a layer where no node qualifies warns.

## What this does not do yet

* **No self-loops.** A link with `from == to` cannot be drawn in 0.1.0.
  It is dropped when the layout is built, with a message:
  `Dropped 1 self-link (from == to); ggcircos 0.1.0 does not draw them.`
  Asking for `self_loops = TRUE` is an error.
* **No label collision avoidance.** `geom_node_text()` puts one label on
  each node and nothing checks whether the labels fit. Short nodes next to
  each other produce overlapping text.
* **No filled-and-outlined density.** `"violin"` fills the outline and
  `"density"` strokes the open curve; there is no single geometry that draws
  a closed shape with both a visible fill and a visible edge (map `colour =`
  on `"violin"` for that).
* **No axis on the angular direction.** `geom_track_axis()` is a radial
  ruler. There are no ticks along the ring and no angular axis, and the
  angular scale is fixed by the layout to `[0, 2 * pi]`.
